body.heading: Your fingers are place values
paragraphs: Hold up one hand. Give each finger a value: thumb 1, index finger 2, middle finger 4, ring finger 8, little finger 16. Each value doubles the one before — this is binary, the counting system computers use, where every position is worth twice the previous one.

To show a number, raise exactly the fingers whose values add up to it. Five is thumb plus middle finger (1 + 4). Thirteen is thumb, middle and ring (1 + 4 + 8). All five fingers raised is 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 — the highest this hand can count.

body.heading: Reading a hand
paragraphs: Practise reading as well as showing. If a friend raises only the index and little fingers, that is 2 + 16 = 18. Only the ring finger? Just 8. No fingers at all is zero — the hand is never empty of meaning.

The reason it works is the same reason ordinary counting works: in decimal, positions are worth 1, 10, 100; in binary, positions are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Every whole number has exactly one recipe of these values, so every number from 0 to 31 has exactly one hand sign.

body.heading: Count something real
paragraphs: Use it for a week: count laps, pages, sips or push-ups on your fingers, resetting only when you pass 31. Two hands extend the range to 1,023 — a party fact worth the practice it takes to get fluent.
And the next time someone says computers think in ones and zeros, look at your hand. You can now do a small piece of what they do, with equipment you were born with.

takeaway: Give each finger a doubling value — 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 — and one hand counts all the way to 31.
